passage:
Rashmi scrolled through her phone in the office pantry, showing everyone screenshots. "Twelve percent in a week. Guaranteed. The group mentor picks the stocks."
Kamal laughed it off the first day. By Thursday, three colleagues had joined. By Friday he felt like the only fool left out.
He put in 10,000 through the group's app. Two days later, 1,400 profit landed in his bank. Real money. His chest went warm.
The mentor messaged him personally: "VIP slot open, only for serious members. Minimum two lakh, doubled returns. Closes tonight."
Kamal moved his emergency savings at 11:40 p.m.
For a week the app showed his balance climbing beautifully. When he tried to withdraw, it asked for a tax clearance fee. Then the group went silent. Then the app vanished.
At the next desk, Rashmi was staring at her own screen, pale.

qa.q: How much profit landed in Kamal's bank after two days?
qa.a: 1,400 profit landed in his bank.

qa.q: Why did Kamal move his emergency savings at 11:40 p.m.?
qa.a: He felt left out as colleagues joined, and the small real payout made him trust the scheme, so fear of missing the closing slot pushed him.

qa.q: Where was the turning point at which Kamal could have stopped?
qa.a: It was the VIP message demanding a large deposit by tonight; pausing, checking whether the scheme was registered and talking to someone independent could have exposed the pressure.

qa.q: What might Rashmi be feeling as she stares at her screen?
qa.a: Rashmi is likely shocked and guilty, realising she has lost money too and drew colleagues in.

grounding: A young man is drawn by screenshots of gains and fear of missing out, trusts a small payout, then loses his savings in a larger deposit.

passage:
"Jyoti, see this," Rajni said at the colony gate, thrusting her phone forward. "Crypto group. I put in twenty thousand, got four thousand back in ten days. Guaranteed."
"Guaranteed? Nothing's guaranteed, Rajni."
"This is. The admin is a real expert. There are photos of him with a big car. Half the colony has joined."
"How do you take money out?"
"You can! Small amounts. Look, this is my withdrawal." She showed another screenshot.
Jyoti chewed her lip. Her savings sat in the bank earning almost nothing. The whole colony seemed to be getting richer except her.
"The admin says new members only till Sunday," Rajni added. "After that, closed."
"Why would a real expert need to hurry us?"
"Arre, you think too much. You'll regret it when we're all buying flats."
Jyoti walked home with the link in her messages, unclicked, her heart racing.

qa.q: How much did Rajni say she got back in ten days?
qa.a: Rajni said she got four thousand back in ten days.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling as she walked home with the unclicked link?
qa.a: She felt torn and anxious, her heart racing with fear of missing out while she doubted the guarantee and the hurry.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do before deciding about the link?
qa.a: She could leave it unclicked, check whether the scheme is registered with the regulator, and talk to someone independent she trusts.

qa.q: How does Rajni see Jyoti's questions?
qa.a: Rajni sees them as overthinking, because the small withdrawal has convinced her the scheme is real.

grounding: A woman is drawn by Rajni's screenshots, an early payout and a closing deadline, and feels fear of missing out while doubting the guarantee.

passage:
In the office canteen in Bengaluru, Aditi scrolled through screenshots for Joseph: green numbers, big percentages, a trading group with thousands of members. "Forty percent in a month, Joseph. Guaranteed. The mentor picks everything."
Joseph was nearly twenty-five, still sharing a flat, watching everyone around him buy cars. His stomach did a nervous flip. What if everyone got rich and he didn't?
He joined the group that night and deposited ₹10,000 through the app. In a week, it showed ₹13,500. He withdrew ₹2,000, and it actually arrived in his bank. He felt a rush of relief. It was real.
The next message from the mentor came on Friday: "Special VIP round. Minimum ₹2 lakh. Only 24 hours. Don't miss this."
Joseph looked at his savings account. Two lakh was almost everything he had. His finger hovered over the transfer button. Something about "only 24 hours" made his chest tight.

qa.q: How much did Joseph withdraw that actually arrived in his bank?
qa.a: He withdrew ₹2,000, and it actually arrived in his bank.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when Aditi showed him the screenshots?
qa.a: Joseph felt nervous and afraid of missing out, worried everyone else would get rich except him.

qa.q: What should Joseph do before transferring any more money?
qa.a: Pause, not rush for the 24-hour deadline, check whether the scheme is registered with the official regulator, and talk to someone independent.

qa.q: How might Aditi see the trading group?
qa.a: Aditi seems to trust it fully, perhaps because she has also seen early gains, without noticing the warning signs.

grounding: It shows an adult drawn by screenshots of big gains, feeling fear of missing out, and early small payouts building trust before a large deposit is asked.

passage:
"Tenzin, just look. Look at my returns." Sudha turned her phone around. "I put in ₹20,000 in March. It's ₹31,000 now."
"How?"
"It's an app. There's a group. The mentor says it's guaranteed. I even took some out, and it came to my account."
Tenzin felt the pull. Rent had just gone up. Everyone in the group looked so happy.
"What's the catch?"
"No catch! But there's a special round this week. Bigger deposit, bigger returns. It closes Sunday. Don't tell too many people, they want to keep it small."
"Why keep it small?"
"So it stays profitable. Come on, Tenzin. Don't be the one who missed out."
Tenzin hesitated. The words "guaranteed," "closes Sunday" and "don't tell" sat strangely together.
"Let me think till tomorrow," Tenzin said.
Sudha rolled her eyes. "By tomorrow it might be full."

qa.q: How much had Sudha put in in March?
qa.a: ₹20,000 in March.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling while Sudha talked?
qa.a: Tenzin felt tempted and anxious about missing out, especially with rent going up, but also uneasy about the words used.

qa.q: What would you advise Tenzin to do next?
qa.a: Take the extra day, check with the official regulator whether the app is registered, and talk to someone independent before deciding.

qa.q: How does Sudha see the scheme?
qa.a: Sudha trusts it because it paid out once, and sees Tenzin's caution as missing a chance.

grounding: It shows an adult pulled by a friend's big gains and early payouts toward a secretive scheme, feeling fear of missing out.

passage:
I'm Kunal, and last year I learned how the trap works from the inside.
My friend Kalyani added me to a trading group. The screenshots were unbelievable. Members posted "₹50k profit today!" with party emojis. A mentor called "Sir" gave tips every morning. Returns were "guaranteed."
I started with ₹5,000. In two weeks it showed ₹9,000. I withdrew ₹3,000, and it came straight to my bank. That was the moment I trusted it completely.
So I added ₹1.5 lakh. My savings. Then more, when they said my account needed "tax clearance" to withdraw.
Then the group went silent. The app stopped opening. Kalyani lost money too.
I felt stupid and scared. But the first small payout was designed to make me feel exactly what I felt: safe. Now, whenever someone says "guaranteed," I think of that ₹3,000. It was the most expensive money I ever received.

qa.q: How much did Kunal withdraw that actually arrived?
How did Kunal feel after the early withdrawal?
qa.a: Kunal felt safe and trusting, exactly as the scheme had been designed to make people feel.

qa.q: What would have protected Kunal?
qa.a: Treating "guaranteed" returns as a warning, checking registration with the official regulator, and reporting early to the cyber police.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel after the group vanished?
qa.a: Kalyani would likely feel guilty for adding Kunal and upset about losing money too.

grounding: An adult recalls how screenshots and early small payouts built trust in a fake trading scheme before larger deposits were lost.

passage:
Supervisor's note, accounts team, Monday.
For two weeks Zubin has been checking a group chat between tasks. Today he showed me screenshots: people posting "guaranteed profit every month" and photos of new bikes. He said he had put in a small amount first and got it back with profit within days, "so it's proven". He is now thinking of putting in his wedding savings before "the window closes Friday". He looked flushed and restless, and said everyone in the group is getting rich except him.
I didn't argue about numbers. I told him an early payout is often how these schemes win people over before bigger sums vanish, and asked whether the platform was registered with the regulator. He didn't know. I suggested he speak to an independent registered adviser, and to his family, before Friday, and I shared the regulator's public warning list.
He agreed to wait. I will check in with him on Wednesday.
Gurleen

qa.q: What happened with Zubin's first small amount?
qa.a: He got it back with profit within days.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling as he talked about the group?
qa.a: Zubin seemed restless and anxious about missing out, flushed and convinced everyone was getting rich except him.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that helped, without giving financial advice?
qa.a: Gurleen explained how early payouts build trust, asked about regulator registration, pointed Zubin to an independent registered adviser and his family, and planned a check-in.

qa.q: How might Zubin's family be affected if he rushed in before Friday?
qa.a: They could lose the wedding savings and face stress and shame, so including them before any decision protects them too.

grounding: Shows a person drawn in by screenshots of big gains, a small early payout and a deadline, feeling fear of missing out.
